what: A feature flag is an if-statement whose answer comes from a remote service, so you can turn features on for some users, ramp them up gradually, run A/B tests, or switch them off instantly without redeploying. On the client you must deal with flicker, security of the flag data, and cleaning up old flags.
like: Like a classroom light switch panel the head teacher controls: you can brighten one row of lamps (a group of users) at a time, and flip them all off if something sparks.
why: Ship code dark, release to users later: deploy and release become separate steps
Gradual rollout and a kill switch shrink the blast radius of a bad change
Experiments let you measure impact instead of guessing

nodes.t: Client SDK|context in, flag value out

steps.d: Each flag has a key, a default, targeting rules (user, plan, country) and a rollout percentage, all edited in the flag service, not in code.
The SDK sends a user context (id, plan, device) and gets back values. Client-side SDKs usually receive only the results, not your rules, so rule details stay off the device.
Fetching flags after load shows the wrong variant for a moment. Evaluate on the server and bootstrap the values into the HTML or SDK so the first paint is correct; the later fetch replaces them.

steps.t: Use the flag in the UI
steps.d: Check the flag at one clear point per feature, always with a safe default for when the service is unreachable.
Log an exposure event when the user actually sees the variant, not when the flag loads. Experiment results depend on this.
A kill switch flips the feature off in seconds through streaming or polling. Release flags are temporary: give each an owner and a removal date.

numbers.l: OpenFeature, the vendor-neutral feature flag API, is an incubating project at the Cloud Native Computing Foundation
Client-side ID for browsers and mobile keys vs a server SDK key, never to be used in client-side code
OpenFeature concepts to know: provider, evaluation context, hooks

choices.d: Server-side evaluation keeps rules private and avoids flicker but needs a request path. Client-side SDKs are flexible for SPAs but add a network fetch and expose evaluated values to users, so never put secrets in flags.
Bootstrap values from the server for a correct first paint; fetch-only is simpler but flashes the wrong variant (the 'flash of control').
Streaming gives near-instant kill switches; polling is simpler and cheaper but lags by the interval. Some SDKs only stream when a change listener is registered.
OpenFeature gives one API with swappable providers, hooks and a shared evaluation context, reducing lock-in at the cost of a thin extra layer.

instead.why: For user-visible filters and modes, URL state is the right tool, not flags
Flags are usually exposed to components through a provider backed by a store

breaks.d: UI renders the default, then swaps after the flag fetch.
breaks.see: Layout shift or flash of control; worse LCP and CLS
breaks.fix: Server bootstrap, skeleton until ready, or evaluate before render

breaks.d: SDK cannot reach the service at startup.
breaks.see: All features fall back to defaults or the app hangs
breaks.fix: Safe defaults, cached last-known values, short init timeout, and a bundled snapshot

breaks.d: Dozens of old flags and nested conditions nobody dares remove.
breaks.see: Untestable combinations and dead code paths
breaks.fix: Owner and expiry per flag, remove after full rollout, lint or report on stale flags

say: Flags decouple deploy from release: I evaluate them for a user context, roll out by percentage, and keep a kill switch with a safe default if the service is down.
To avoid flicker I evaluate on the server and bootstrap the values into the page, so the first paint is right and the client SDK just takes over.
I log exposure events when the user sees a variant, treat release flags as temporary with an owner and removal date, and never put secrets in a client-visible flag.

followups.q: How does a percentage rollout stay consistent for a user?
followups.a: The service hashes the user id with the flag key into a bucket, so the same user gets the same answer every time, and raising the percentage only adds users.

followups.q: How do you test code behind flags?
followups.a: Unit test both branches by setting the flag in a test provider, run key end-to-end flows with the new variant, and keep the number of live combinations small by removing flags quickly.

followups.q: What is the risk of client-side flags?
followups.a: Users can see evaluated values and tamper with the client, so never use a flag as the only security gate; enforce permissions on the server too.

today: OpenFeature, a CNCF incubating project, gives a vendor-neutral API with providers, evaluation context and hooks, including web client SDKs. Vendors support server-side bootstrapping so client-side flags and experiments no longer need to flash the wrong variant.

check.q: Best way to stop users seeing the wrong variant for a moment?
check.a: Evaluate on the server and bootstrap flag values into the client
d: Hide the whole page with a long timeout
Store flags in a cookie forever
check.why: Bootstrapping gives the SDK correct values at startup; the later fetch just refreshes them.

check.q: What should an experiment log when the user sees a variant?
d: Nothing, it is derived on the server
check.why: Exposure events tie outcomes to who actually saw each variant.

check.q: Which statement about client-side flag SDKs is true?
check.a: They receive evaluation results, so never put secrets in flags
d: They receive the full targeting rules
They can use the server SDK key safely
Their values cannot be changed by a user
check.why: Client-visible values can be inspected and tampered with, so enforce real access control on the server.
